An indexed pension can still lose purchasing power: chart the cap and the spending gap

Use four graphics to compare fixed, capped and fully inflation-matched annual income in future dollars and starting-year purchasing power.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore fixed, capped and fully inflation-matched income

Interactive planning lab

Hypothetical gross annual pension and separate spending basket, with constant assumed inflation. Starting year is index 0; each later index adds one completed annual increase. Fixed income grows 0%; capped indexing uses the lower of selected inflation and cap; full matching uses selected inflation. No plan entitlement, taxes, mortality, survivor change, bridge-benefit expiry, investment return or funding portfolio is calculated.

The central idea

An annual pension increase and preservation of purchasing power are different measures. Compare the increase formula with the spending basket it needs to support.

01

Read the adjustment formula, not just the word indexed

Two pensions with the same opening payment can develop very different purchasing power. One might remain fixed; another might receive annual increases subject to a ceiling. The word “indexed” alone does not identify the amount, timing or conditions of an adjustment.

The FCAC’s employer-pension overview explains that a defined benefit pension may increase to help cover rising living costs and directs members to their administrator to confirm indexing. This guide does not apply a particular pension plan’s rules.

The tool creates three original comparison paths. Fixed income receives no annual increase. Capped income increases by the lower of the selected inflation assumption and the entered cap. The full-match reference increases at the selected inflation rate. Real plans can use different reference periods, partial indexing, conditional increases or other formulas; replace the illustration with confirmed plan terms before relying on a projection.

02

Start all three income paths at the same amount

The default starts with CAD 36,000 of gross annual pension income and a separate CAD 36,000 annual spending basket. Inflation is assumed constant at 3%, while the capped path has a 2% annual ceiling. Every path starts at index zero with the same income amount.

After twenty-five completed annual increases, fixed income remains CAD 36,000. Capped income reaches about CAD 59,061.82, while the full-match reference reaches CAD 75,376.01. The first chart shows those nominal annual amounts, rather than cumulative lifetime payments.

The capped amount is visibly larger than its starting amount. That is useful information about the number of dollars received, but it does not establish that the pension buys more. The spending basket has also risen. The index convention matters: the point labelled twenty-five includes twenty-five increases; it is not the twenty-fifth payment with only twenty-four increases.

03

Translate the income back into starting-year dollars

The second chart divides each future annual income by the assumed price-level increase. Its rule is real income at year t = nominal income at year t ÷ (1 + inflation)t. Both income and prices use the same completed-year count.

At the default horizon, CAD 36,000 of fixed annual income buys about what CAD 17,193.80 bought at the start. The capped path’s CAD 59,061.82 buys about CAD 28,208.25 in starting-year terms. Its purchasing power has fallen by about 21.64%, even though the nominal payment has increased.

The full-match reference retains CAD 36,000 of starting-year purchasing power because its assumed income growth exactly matches the modeled price increase. This is a mathematical control, rather than a promise about a plan or the household’s actual inflation experience. Do not reduce the real amounts by inflation a second time.

04

Measure an annual funding gap without inventing a portfolio

The selected spending basket reaches about CAD 75,376.01 after twenty-five increases. Against the capped annual pension, this creates a positive annual difference of about CAD 16,314.19 in that future year’s dollars. The third chart compares spending, income and that difference side by side.

The gap calculation is max(spending − income, zero). When entered income exceeds spending, the reported positive gap is zero. The model does not assume that any excess is saved, invested or carried forward to meet later costs.

These are gross pension amounts and an independently entered spending basket. They are not a complete after-tax retirement cash plan. Income tax can widen the resources needed for spending, while other pensions, savings or work income could help fund it. The chart also does not convert one future annual shortfall into a required lump sum; that calculation needs the full sequence of withdrawals, returns, costs and available resources.

05

Read the inflation-and-cap matrix as a sensitivity test

The matrix holds starting pension income and the horizon fixed. Its rows replace constant inflation and its columns replace the annual cap. Each cell shows the capped income at the horizon in starting-year dollars, allowing different nominal paths to be compared on one purchasing-power basis.

A cap at or above assumed inflation preserves starting purchasing power in this formula. Raising the cap further has no additional effect because the modeled annual increase cannot exceed inflation. A zero cap reproduces the fixed-income case.

These cells are alternatives, not probabilities or official inflation forecasts. The Bank of Canada’s inflation explanation provides context for price measurement. A household’s mix of housing, care, travel and other expenses can differ from an aggregate index. The scenario deliberately keeps quantities fixed to isolate prices; a change in lifestyle or care needs belongs in a separate spending adjustment.

06

Put the purchasing-power question into the retirement review

Request the pension’s actual indexing formula, its first adjustment date and any cap or conditions. Check whether a quoted benefit includes a temporary component that later ends. A payment reduction or survivor change should not be hidden inside an inflation assumption.

Build a starting spending basket from the household’s own records and state whether it is before or after tax. Compare major expenses that may evolve differently. Then add separately verified income sources on their actual schedules rather than applying one indexing assumption to the whole household.

This tool excludes mortality and assumes the selected annual amount remains payable throughout the horizon. It does not value the pension, estimate a transfer value or compare a lump sum with pension payments. Its narrower purpose is to show why a rising nominal payment can coexist with falling purchasing power and a growing annual spending gap.
